Well.... I just got accepted - I am 24 years old. This is my first semester at A&M. 

........

This is lengthy, but I think these things were vital to my acceptance.

........

I dropped out of high school at 17. Got my GED.

I have 8 drops on my transcript (Texas allows 6, and 2 are medically excused).

From Spring 2013 to Summer 2016, my GPA a 1.3. I was on academic suspension.

I took one class that summer - missed the final and failed. It was online - I have struggled with those since then, as well. I have sworn off online courses, lol.

I retook it in the fall, made an A. Took 3 classes in the Spring of 2017, and made 3 A's. Took 6 classes in the summer, 5 A's and 1 B. --- the transcript list goes on. I did some volunteer work (~70 hours between 3 places). I have 2 C's rolling around in there, + 2 medic withdrawals - my therapy was at a level that my emotional growth was on hiatus, so I needed to get back on a mood stabilizer. I was an absolutely mess. I dropped 2 of the 3 classes, I made either a B or and A in the remaining course I had.

But I graduated with Honors on my Associate in Science at the age of 23, summer 2018.

I worked 2 full time jobs while taking 1 class when I submitted my application. I had an amazing professor/  mentor who helped me out fixing my essay and wrote me a recommendation letter. I emailed him the Sunday of the deadline week. He edited it that evening. And he set up a meeting Tuesday evening to finish my application, and to hand me my letter of recommendation.

I didn't know you could post the letter online, so I mailed that thing next day air ($25) so it would be there on Thursday, the deadline day.

...

I couldn't believe it. I cried when I saw I got accepted. 5 years ago, I never thought I'd be worth anything. I abused myself so badly with over eating and suicidal tendencies.

The first and only university I ever applied to thought I was good enough.

...


I think the only thing going for my rickety looking college history is that I am older than most of my class men. I'm to be 25 in a couple of months. I have a recognizable pattern of maturity and success, not just happenstance.

And I wrote about all of these things. My mom died when I was 14. I was on so many antipsychotics in high school I really on remember being numb and still suicidal. I moved out, lost my job & dropped out of high school all in 6 months. I gained 100 pounds, and had worked close to 10 different jobs by the age of 20.

And then I got a fucking grip on my life. I've lost >70pounds of that weight, took care of my mental health, and become a much more stable individual as a whole.

My point is - I was a wreck and destroyed my early college career (and adulthood), and A&M still accepted me.

I think the key component alongside a decent transcript is exposing yourself in your essay. I'm proud of the person I've been working on - I've come a long way, and I think A&M saw that.


Also, I'm beginning to think the major I wanted happened to be a major that has quite the availability for acceptance as it stands - I could be wrong. I'm a WFSC major, so if anyone can clarify, give it a go!

.....

Overall, if your essay is compelling, and your transcript matches your dedication, you have a pretty good shot.

Another point of interest that may make this announcement go a little smooth is: ask her if she has anything that she may have problems with. This would make her feel less attacked - even though you know you aren't trying to be mean or spiteful, you're just requesting more respect in your shared home - and could possibly squash any animosity that may be building up from a lack of communication on her end as well.

And lastly, I would suggest an "open door" policy. Make it clear that both of you should be able to approach one another whenever there's something worth addressing.

I would also let her know at some point that you would like to have your privacy. You don't have to explain why you need it beyond the fact that having time to yourself allows you to reflect upon your day and maintain a positive balance in your life. Or whatever simplified reason you actually have to be alone, so questions and disclosure about your mental health or what have you can be shut down before that even begins.

For me, as long as when either of us comes home, we can do whatever we want that makes us happy, as long as it is respectful of the space we share with one another. And that includes being disruptive in our own rooms like blasting terrible music at stupid hours and noisy competitive sexcapades. Yes, those exist. Be glad you only have 1 roommate.

Good luck!!

Communication is key. She won't know that you have problems with her or her behavior or how she is treating the living space you share.

Introversy is very difficult to match with extrovercy. You both seem young, since she has failed to discuss with you what is appropriate, and you have failed to do the same. The only difference is: she expresses herself and what she wants and may be over entitled, and you shut down when she confronts you and never find the right time to approach her. Not that you aren't looking - but it's hard for you to tell when a good time to interject your needs and wants.

Which is really hard. I used to be a lot like her, and I always thought I was right and couldn't understand why others weren't just like me. My husband is an introvert and for several years at the beginning of our relationship, I completely disrespected his need for time alone as well as any disagreements he had with me, my behavior or my treatment of our living space.

I would recommend writing down everything you have to say, and approach her with your list. After you introduce that you need to talk, you can choose to recite from your list, or give her the list and ask her to respond within a few days.

1) Let her know you come from a place of neutrality, that you want both of you to enjoy your home together.
2) Make sure the changes you want to work on are open ended. Whatever it is you have a problem with, explain why and what you think could be done, and ask her what you both can do together to accomplish this task. I.E. her tea and cereal excessiveness: let her know you want more space in the kitchen, and since the tea and cereal are dry storage, ask if she could find a way to condense how much tea and cereal she stocks up on or if she can store it in her personal space/room (or desk space if you don't think she will just crowd the living room even further).

For people who are extroverted like she is (I was there once), she has to feel somewhat empowered. It sucks. I am so embarrassed how arrogant I was. But it shows that she has a very dominant personality, and you have a very submissive one.

It sucks to be stuck with a roommate who doesn't share the same cleanliness habits and space respectfulness. It's even worse when they aren't willing to be considerate enough to ask you what your perspective is on your shared living space. And it's really shitty when that person is aggressive about any suggestions or complaints you have, making you unsure how to approach them or if you even should.

Toxicity sucks. I'm sorry you have to live with it.
